passage:
Last term I was the new boy in 9B, and I learnt fast who owned the back bench by the window. Mahima, Sharmila and three others shared tiffins, notes and inside jokes. When Sharmila forgot the group chart, Mahima said, "She had a family function, poor thing," and they redid it together at lunch.
Two weeks later I was the one who forgot my part of the science model. Mahima rolled her eyes. "Typical. Some people just don't care." Sharmila told Sir I was "never serious." Nobody asked why. My grandfather had been in hospital that week.
I'm Kunal, and I still remember how hot my ears felt, standing there, knowing the same mistake had two different prices depending on which bench you sat on.

qa.q: What did Kunal forget two weeks after Sharmila forgot the group chart?
qa.a: Kunal forgot his part of the science model.

qa.q: Why did Kunal's ears feel hot as he stood there?
qa.a: He felt ashamed and angry: Sharmila's lapse was excused with sympathy, while his identical one was called not caring, and nobody asked his reason.

qa.q: When the group turned on Kunal in front of Sir, what choice could he have made in that moment?
qa.a: He could calmly tell Sir that his grandfather had been in hospital that week, so his side is heard instead of only the group's verdict.

qa.q: How might Sharmila see her own forgotten chart differently from Kunal's forgotten model?
qa.a: To Sharmila, her lapse had a good reason because her friends explained it for her; Kunal's looks like carelessness because no one in the group knows or asks about his week.

grounding: A teenage boy outside a back-bench group sees them excuse one member's lapse while condemning his identical one.

passage:
Class 10C, note after the Thursday inter-house match.
Pranav came off the field quietly today. During the match, Ishita's friends laughed off two missed passes by Dev, one of their own: "Pitch is bumpy." When Pranav slipped and lost the ball, the same group shouted that he was "useless" and "shouldn't even be on the team." I saw him stare at the ground and walk to the far end of the bench, away from everyone. On the walk back, Ishita said he had "ruined it for all of us."
Afterwards I sat with Pranav. He said, "When they miss, it's the pitch. When I miss, it's me." I told him I had seen both moments and that it was not a fair way to judge anyone. Tomorrow I will talk to the whole team about one rule for everyone on the field.
— Ms Rao, class teacher

qa.q: What did the group say when Dev missed two passes?
qa.a: They laughed it off and said, "Pitch is bumpy."

qa.q: What does Pranav's walk to the far end of the bench suggest about how he felt?
qa.a: It suggests he felt hurt and shut out, sure the group would never judge him as kindly as they judged Dev. 😔

qa.q: What choice did Ms Rao make after the match, and why does it matter?
qa.a: Ms Rao chose to sit with Pranav and tell him both moments were seen, so he knew the double standard was real and not in his head.

qa.q: If you were Dev, how might it feel to watch Pranav blamed for a smaller mistake than yours?
qa.a: Dev might feel uneasy or guilty, realising the group covered for the two missed passes and aimed all the anger at Pranav instead.

grounding: A teacher records how a clique excuses its own player's misses but harshly blames Pranav, the boy outside it.

passage:
Tuesday night
Today in the library group project, Mehak copied two paragraphs straight from a website. Disha just said, "Chill, everyone does it, she was tired." Then I suggested a different title for our poster and Disha said, loud enough for the next table, "Here comes that boy who thinks he's smart." Mehak laughed.
They have a group chat, the four of them, and I'm not in it, so decisions happen before I even reach school. When I pointed out the copying, suddenly I was "a snitch" and "not a team player."
I don't even want to be in their group. I just want the same rules. If Mehak can be tired, why can't I be right?
Anyway. Maths homework still not done.
— Farhan

qa.q: What did Mehak copy from a website?
qa.a: Mehak copied two paragraphs straight from a website.

qa.q: What is Farhan wishing for when he writes 'I just want the same rules'?
qa.a: Farhan feels excluded and hurt, and wants fairness more than friendship: to be judged by the rules Disha and Mehak use for each other, not a harsher set kept for him.

qa.q: Farhan has to decide what to do about the copied paragraphs before the poster goes in. Which choice would help him most?
qa.a: He could quietly tell the teacher that parts of the poster were copied and ask for his own section to be marked separately, instead of arguing with the group again.

qa.q: How might Disha see Farhan's point about the copying?
qa.a: Because Disha already treats Mehak as one of the group who was just tired, Farhan's point may look like an attack on the group rather than a fair concern.

grounding: A teenage boy outside a four-person clique notices they excuse a member's copying while calling him a snitch.

passage:
In the kasba school near Sagar, the cricket team was really a group of five boys who had grown up in the same lane. Vishal, fifteen, had moved there from another village in June. He bowled better than most of them, but they picked him last, if at all.
On Saturday, Rajni, the sports captain, watched it happen. When Deepak, one of the five, dropped two easy catches, the others slapped his back. "Unlucky, yaar." When Vishal misfielded once, the same boys groaned loudly. "Village-boy hands."
"You're from a village too," Vishal muttered, but no one heard.
He walked home the long way, kicking stones. His mother asked if the match went well. "Fine," he said, and went straight to the roof, where he bowled at the water tank alone until it was dark.
On Monday, Rajni wrote the fielding errors in the scorebook for every player, with names.

qa.q: How many boys made up the cricket group?
qa.a: It was a group of five boys who had grown up in the same lane.

qa.q: What does Vishal bowling alone at the water tank until dark suggest about how he felt?
qa.a: It suggests he felt hurt and shut out, still loving the game but not wanting to talk about how unfairly he had been treated.

qa.q: How might Rajni's scorebook change things for Vishal?
qa.a: Writing every player's fielding errors with names makes the record the same for everyone, so Deepak's dropped catches and Vishal's misfield are judged by one rule.

qa.q: What was it like for Vishal to hear 'Village-boy hands' after Deepak was told 'Unlucky, yaar'?
qa.a: For Vishal it showed that the group excused its own and judged him harshly for less, which is why he muttered that they were from a village too.

grounding: It shows a teenage boy outside a village cricket clique watching members excuse each other while he is judged harshly for smaller slips.

passage: In Class 9 there was the back-bench group, and there was me. Akash and his four friends did everything together: lunch, cricket, the same jokes. When Akash forgot his homework, they said, "Sir gives too much anyway." When one of them copied in the unit test, it was "just helping each other." But when I forgot my lab coat once, Akash announced to the class, "Ujjwal is so careless." When I got a question wrong, they laughed for a full minute. Same mistakes, different rules. I stopped raising my hand. What hurt wasn't only the laughing. It was seeing how gently they treated each other, and knowing I would never get that. That year taught me what loyalty looks like from the outside: a locked door.

qa.q: What did Akash say when Ujjwal forgot the lab coat?
qa.a: "Ujjwal is so careless."

qa.q: Why did Ujjwal feel so hurt that year?
qa.a: Ujjwal felt hurt and shut out, seeing how gently the group treated each other while Ujjwal was judged harshly for the same mistakes.

qa.q: What could a teacher or classmate do if they noticed this pattern?
qa.a: Point out the double standard calmly, apply the same rules to everyone, and bring Ujjwal into group work so the door opens a little.

qa.q: How might Akash's group see their own behaviour?
qa.a: They probably see it as normal loyalty to friends, without noticing how unfair it feels to someone outside.

grounding: A teenager recalls being outside a clique that excused its own members' slips while judging the same slips harshly in the outsider.

passage:
Class teacher's note, Class 11B, 18 November
Jatin joined us in August from another city and has not been let into any group. This week I noticed a pattern. When Trisha's group came back late from the canteen, the class monitor, who is part of it, wrote nothing. When Jatin came in two minutes late on Wednesday, she wrote his name on the board. During the group presentation, Trisha's friends praised each other's slides and called Jatin's section "confusing," though it was the clearest. He sat very still afterwards and skipped lunch. Today he asked me quietly if he could do the next project alone. I said I would think about it. I will speak to the monitor about applying the late rule equally, and I will set the next groups myself.

qa.q: What did the monitor do when Jatin came in two minutes late?
qa.a: Wrote his name on the board.

qa.q: Why did Jatin ask to do the next project alone?
qa.a: He felt hurt and excluded, seeing the group excuse each other while judging his clear work as confusing.

qa.q: What steps is the teacher taking, and why do they help?
qa.a: Asking the monitor to apply the late rule equally and setting the next groups, so the same rules apply to all and Jatin isn't left outside.

qa.q: How might Trisha's group see their comments on Jatin's section?
qa.a: They may think they were being honest, without noticing they judged him more harshly than their own friends.

grounding: A teacher records a new boy outside a clique being judged harshly for things the group excuses in its own members.

passage:
Sunday night
Two months in the hostel and I've figured out the rules. There's Pema's corridor group, and there's everyone else. When one of them plays music till two, it's "just relaxing." When I played mine at ten, Pema banged on my door and said I had no manners. When their room was messy at inspection, they laughed about it together. When mine had one shirt on the chair, I got called lazy in the corridor.
I'm not even angry today. I'm just tired. It's like they have a softer pair of eyes for each other and a harder one for me.
Tomorrow I'm going to talk to the warden. Not to complain about them. Just to ask if the rules can be written on the board, for everyone.
Chaitanya

qa.q: What did Pema say when Chaitanya played music at ten?
qa.a: That Chaitanya had no manners.

qa.q: How is Chaitanya feeling tonight?
qa.a: Chaitanya feels tired and hurt rather than angry, sensing the group has softer eyes for each other and harder ones for outsiders.

qa.q: What does Chaitanya plan, and why is it a fair step?
qa.a: Asking the warden to write the rules on the board for everyone, which aims at equal rules rather than attacking the group.

qa.q: How might Pema's group see the music and mess rules?
qa.a: They probably see their own behaviour as ordinary relaxing and don't notice they judge Chaitanya by a stricter standard.

grounding: A hostel diary shows an outsider noticing a group excusing its own members while judging the outsider harshly for the same things.

passage: Manoj had joined the Class 9 at the government school in Karjat in July, after his father's transfer. The boys who had been together since Class 1 sat on the last three benches and moved as one. When one of them forgot his homework, the others said, "Sir, his grandmother was ill." passage: In Oslo, Omar's group project was due the same day as everyone else's. His was a day late because the printer broke. The popular group at the back of the class, four friends since kindergarten, handed theirs in two days late. When the teacher asked, one of them said, "We had a family thing," and the others nodded, and that was that. When Omar explained about the printer, one of the four laughed. "Sure. Printer ate your homework." Later, in the corridor, Omar heard them say he was "lazy, just like we thought." He walked home in the grey drizzle, not answering his mother's texts. Ingrid, the girl who sat next to him in maths, caught up at the bus stop. "They were two days late," she said. "I saw." Omar just shrugged. It didn't feel like enough.

qa.q: Why was Omar's project a day late?
qa.a: Because the printer broke.

qa.q: What was Omar feeling as he walked home?
qa.a: He felt hurt and discouraged, not answering texts, because the group excused their own lateness but called him lazy.

qa.q: What would you advise Omar to do next?
qa.a: Tell his mother or the teacher about the double standard, with the dates, rather than carrying it alone.

qa.q: How does Ingrid see what happened?
qa.a: Ingrid sees the unfairness clearly, noticing the group was two days late while Omar was only one.

grounding: Shows a teenager outside a clique whose members excuse their own lateness while mocking him for less.

Kunal slid into the debate room at 4:02, breathless from the stairs. Ankita, sitting with her usual group of four by the window, didn't look up from her notes. "Some people treat practice like a hobby," one of them said, loud enough.
Kunal sat at the far end and opened his folder. His cheeks burned.
At 4:15 the door banged again. Ankita's closest friend walked in, hair wet from the rain, laughing.
"Poor thing, the buses are terrible today," Ankita said, moving her bag so a chair was ready.
Nobody said anything about hobbies.
In the practice round, Kunal made a sharp point about school timings. The window group exchanged looks. When Ankita's friend repeated almost the same point ten minutes later, they clapped.
Kunal stared at his pen and counted the ceiling fan's turns until the bell.

qa.q: What was Kunal feeling when the group clapped for the repeated point?
qa.a: Kunal felt hurt and humiliated, because the same point earned him looks but earned the group's friend applause, as if the rules depended on who you were.

qa.q: How could the debate teacher make practice fairer for someone like Kunal?

Dear Lavanya Didi,
You asked how the new school is. Honestly? Mixed.
There's a group of five boys who have been together since Class 1. They run the cricket nets at lunch. On Tuesday one of them dropped two easy catches. "Sun in his eyes," they said, and patted his back.
On Wednesday I dropped one. The captain said, "Concentrate, yaar, this isn't gully cricket," and they all went quiet at me. Nobody mentioned the sun. It was the same sun.
Yesterday one of them forgot his homework, and the others swore to Ma'am he'd left it on the bus. When I forgot mine last week, they told her I never do it.
I'm not asking you to fix anything. I just needed to tell someone that it feels like there are two rulebooks, one for them and one for me.
Your brother,
Kamal

qa.q: How many easy catches did one of the group drop on Tuesday?
qa.a: One of them dropped two easy catches on Tuesday, and the group said it was the sun in his eyes.

qa.q: Why does the dropped catch on Wednesday sting Kamal so much?
qa.a: Kamal feels hurt and shut out, because the same mistake earned a group member sympathy but earned Kamal a telling-off, so the group seems to judge by who you are.

qa.q: What small step could help Kamal at the new school?
qa.a: Kamal could look for classmates outside the group of five, or mention the pattern to a trusted teacher, so the group's two rulebooks aren't the only measure.

qa.q: How might Lavanya feel reading the letter?
qa.a: Lavanya might feel protective and sad for her brother, and glad that Kamal chose to tell her instead of keeping it inside.

grounding: Shows a new student outside a long-standing group of boys noticing that they excuse each other's slips while judging his.

passage:
Tushar, you asked why I left the school band, so here's the honest version. I'm Varun, the guy who carried the drum kit up three floors every Friday for a whole year. The other four have played together since they were small. When one of them came in late or off-beat, it was "leave it, he's tired, exams na." When I rushed one fill at the Annual Day rehearsal, the lead guitarist said I was ruining the song, and the others nodded.
Then the keyboard player missed a whole verse. They laughed and called it jazz.
I kept thinking, if I'd missed that verse, I'd be out by evening. That's when I understood it was never really about the music. It was about who's already inside.
I'm not angry any more. Just tired of auditioning every week for people who had already decided about me.

qa.q: What did the others call it when the keyboard player missed a whole verse?
qa.a: They laughed and called it jazz.

qa.q: What was Varun feeling when the missed verse was laughed off?
qa.a: Varun felt bitter and left out, because a slip that would have got Varun thrown out was treated as a joke for someone already inside the group.

qa.q: What could Varun try next instead of giving up music altogether?
qa.a: Varun could look for a group where feedback rules are the same for everyone, or ask the music teacher to run open auditions and rehearsals.

qa.q: How might Tushar see Varun's decision to leave the band?
qa.a: Tushar may understand that Varun left for protection from unfair judging, not from any loss of love for the drums, and may want to include Varun more.

grounding: Shows a teenager outside a close band group hearing them excuse each other's mistakes while judging the speaker's harshly.

Monday, the week before Ganesh festival: The class decoration committee was really Urmila's group of five. When Keya from the group spilled glue across the big chart, Urmila laughed. "Accidents happen. Just cover it with glitter." Nilesh, who had been added to the committee late, said nothing and fetched a cloth.
Thursday: Nilesh stapled the paper lanterns a little crooked. "Who let him touch it?" Urmila said loudly. "This is why we don't take outsiders." The group giggled. Nilesh's ears burned, and he stapled the rest in silence.
The next Monday, after the festival: The class teacher praised the committee's work. Urmila's group went up to collect the certificate. Nilesh's name was on the list, but nobody called him. He stayed at his desk, straightening pencils that were already straight, remembering the glue that didn't matter and the staples that did.

qa.q: How did Nilesh feel when Urmila said "This is why we don't take outsiders"?
